4.2.3. Wind
The dynamic property of natural airflow is ubiquitous in the outdoor
environment [30,104] and contributes significantly to the overall
experiential quality of the outdoor environment [72]. To capture the
dynamics of natural wind, a high-speed thermal anemometer was used
to record a 30-min actual wind timeseries at 20 Hz in an urban outdoor
environment. This was then simulated in the indoor climate chamber
using a bank of blade-less fans with stepper-motors that were digitally
controlled to replicate the turbulence characteristics of the outdoor
recording. The breeze simulation device consists of an Arduino micro-
controller, infrared receiver, and infrared transmitting LED. The tem-
poral variation of air velocity was achieved by transforming the air
velocity values into a time sequence of control voltages for the fan at the
respective operating levels. The spatial variation of natural wind within
the semi-outdoor environment can be achieved by assigning different
wind profiles to different zones in the Virtual Reality environment in
Unity 3D. When the subject enters a virtual microclimate zone, a virtual
event will be triggered to send a location-specific wind profile signal to
the fans. The distances of the fans to the subject were determined by the
air velocity measured by a thermal anemometer (TSI 9545A, 1 Hz) at the
highest fan operating level. Fig. 6 shows a sample of the agreement

5.2. Data collection
During the experiment, participants’ physiological responses,
cognitive performance response, behaviours and subjective experience
in MIVE were collected. In terms of physiological response, their
galvanic skin responses, an indication of arousal and psychophysiolog-
ical stress, were continuously monitored using Shimmer3 GSR +Unit
[80] with a sampling frequency of 200 Hz. The effect of environmental
exposure on participants’ cognitive performance was assessed by
cognitive performance tests before and after MIVE exposure. A detailed
description of the cognitive tests is presented in Lyu et al. (2022). Par-
ticipants’ subjective experiences regarding their experience in MIVE
